identity.title: SWE-Lancer: Can Frontier LLMs Earn $1 Million from Real-World Freelance Software Engineering?

problem.claim: The paper asks whether frontier LLMs can perform real-world freelance software engineering tasks and generate substantial monetary value.

contributions.claim: Introduces SWE-Lancer, a benchmark of over 1,400 Upwork software-engineering tasks worth $1 million in aggregate payouts, spanning independent engineering and managerial decisions.
Defines task-specific assessment using end-to-end tests for engineering tasks and comparison with original hired managers’ choices for managerial tasks.
Releases a unified Docker image and public evaluation split to support subsequent research.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors present SWE-Lancer as a benchmark grounded in real freelance software-engineering tasks and mapped to monetary value.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that frontier models remain unable to solve a majority of the benchmark tasks.

narrative_sequence.summary: The paper introduces a benchmark built from over 1,400 real Upwork tasks with $1 million in total stated value.
The benchmark covers independent work from $50 bug fixes to $32,000 feature implementations, plus managerial proposal-selection tasks.
Independent tasks use end-to-end tests triple-verified by experienced software engineers; managerial tasks are assessed against original managers’ decisions.
The authors report that frontier models cannot solve most tasks.
The authors release evaluation infrastructure and frame monetary mapping as a way to study AI development’s economic impact.

source_observation.claim: The abstract aligns task types with distinct evaluation targets: executable tests for implementation and human-manager decisions for managerial judgment.

lessons.interpretation: When a benchmark spans qualitatively different work, matching each task category to its real-world success criterion can make claims more interpretable.
lessons.application: For a mixed-role benchmark, define separate outcome measures tied to the operational criterion of each role before reporting aggregate performance.
lessons.exception: This approach may be unsuitable when task categories lack stable, observable success criteria or comparable reference decisions.

unknowns: The abstract does not identify the evaluated models or report exact per-task, per-category, or monetary performance figures.
It does not specify the construction, coverage, or public availability details of the full dataset beyond the stated evaluation split and Docker image.
The abstract does not establish how monetary value is converted into an aggregate earning estimate.
